title: Rapid Screening of CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing Outcomes in Cell Populations
author: Wilbie, Mastrobattista, et al.
materials: Nikon ECLIPSE ti2-U inverted and fluorescent microscope

steps.title: Prepare cell culture media
steps.instruction: Make three media formulations: (i) Complete medium – add 55.6 mL fetal bovine serum to 500 mL DMEM to obtain 10 % (v/v) FBS; (ii) Antibiotic‑antimycotic medium – add 0.5 mL 100× antibiotic‑antimycotic to 49.5 mL complete medium for a final 1× concentration; (iii) Selection medium – add 10 µL of 10 mg/mL puromycin to 50 mL complete medium to reach 2 µg/mL puromycin.

steps.title: Thaw and seed HEK293T cells
steps.instruction: Rapidly thaw a frozen HEK293T stock, resuspend the cells in 10 mL complete medium in a 15 mL conical tube, centrifuge 5 min at 300 × g, discard supernatant, resuspend the pellet in 15 mL complete medium, transfer to a T75 flask and incubate at 37 °C with 5 % CO₂ for at least one week before any downstream work. If confluency exceeds 80 %, passage as described in the routine culture steps.

steps.title: Maintain and passage HEK293T cultures
steps.instruction: Every 3–4 days, perform the following on a T25 flask (scale volumes proportionally for larger vessels): (a) Aspirate spent medium; (b) Wash cells with 5 mL sterile 1× PBS; (c) Aspirate PBS; (d) Add 0.5 mL Trypsin‑EDTA; (e) Incubate 37 °C for 2–5 min; (f) Verify detachment under a microscope; (g) Add 2.5 mL complete medium to neutralize trypsin and gently pipette up‑and‑down ~10× to obtain a single‑cell suspension; (h) Transfer an appropriate volume to a fresh flask (typically 1:10 split, performed twice weekly); (i) Add 5 mL fresh complete medium to the new flask and return to the incubator.

steps.title: Expand edited cells and re‑plate
steps.instruction: Five days after CRISPR transfection, assess confluency; if >80 % in a 96‑well plate, passage to a 48‑well plate (≈3× surface area). For each well: (i) Aspirate medium; (ii) Wash with 50 µL PBS (avoid direct pipetting onto cells); (iii) Add 30 µL Trypsin‑EDTA; (iv) Incubate 37 °C for 5 min (HEK293T); (v) Dilute trypsin with 80 µL complete medium; (vi) Resuspend by pipetting 5–10×; (vii) Transfer the entire volume to a corresponding well of a 48‑well plate (3× dilution); (viii) Add 400 µL complete medium; (ix) Incubate at 37 °C until a total of 5 days post‑transfection, expanding to larger vessels if needed.

steps.title: Harvest, fix, and resuspend cells
steps.instruction: From the 48‑well plate, perform: (i) Aspirate medium; (ii) Wash with 100 µL PBS; (iii) Add 50 µL Trypsin‑EDTA; (iv) Incubate 37 °C for 5 min (HEK293T); (v) Add 200 µL complete medium and gently resuspend; (vi) Transfer the suspension to a BD Falcon U‑bottom plate; (vii) Centrifuge 500 × g at 18–24 °C for 5 min; (viii) Remove supernatant with a multichannel pipette; (ix) Add 200 µL PBS, resuspend 5×; (x) Centrifuge 500 × g, 5 min; (xi) Remove supernatant; (xii) Add 200 µL 1 % paraformaldehyde, resuspend 5×; (xiii) Incubate 15–30 min at 4 °C; (xiv) Centrifuge 500 × g, 5 min; (xv) Remove supernatant, add 200 µL PBS, resuspend 5×; (xvi) Centrifuge 500 × g, 5 min; (xvii) Remove supernatant, add 200 µL FACS buffer (1 % BSA, 2 mM EDTA in PBS without Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺), resuspend 5×. Use the fixed cells the same day for flow cytometry.

steps.title: Configure flow cytometer and acquire data
steps.instruction: Set up the cytometer according to manufacturer guidelines: use a 488 nm blue laser with a filter near 510 nm for eGFP and a 405 nm violet laser with a filter near 440 nm for BFP; record forward‑scatter (FSC) and side‑scatter (SSC) area and height. Run untreated eGFP⁺ control cells first to place the FSC/SSC cloud centrally, position the eGFP signal in the top 25–30 % of detector range and the BFP signal in the bottom 25–30 %. Apply compensation (≈1–2 % for BD FACS Canto II) by measuring eGFP⁺ cells in the BFP channel. Include a non‑fluorescent (untransduced) control for gating. Acquire at least 10 000 events per sample and save the raw .fsc files. Shut down the instrument as per standard procedure.

steps.title: Gate data and compute editing metrics
steps.instruction: Import the .fcs files into analysis software (e.g., Flowlogic). (a) Gate FSC‑A vs SSC‑A to exclude debris and aggregates; (b) Gate single cells using pulse‑geometry (FSC‑A vs FSC‑H or SSC‑A vs SSC‑H); (c) Plot eGFP vs BFP and create gates: eGFP⁻/BFP⁻ (gene knockout), eGFP⁻/BFP⁺ (gene correction), and eGFP⁺/BFP⁻ (unedited). Verify that BFP⁺ cells are eGFP⁻; if not, allow longer recovery or check for multiple integrations. (d) Subtract the blank percentages obtained from untreated eGFP⁺ controls from both the knockout and correction gates. (e) Define “Absolute gene knockout” = corrected % of eGFP⁻/BFP⁻; “Absolute gene correction” = corrected % of eGFP⁻/BFP⁺. (f) Compute “Total Gene Editing” = absolute knockout + absolute correction. (g) Calculate “Relative gene correction” = (absolute correction / total gene editing) × 100 %. Plot and statistically compare the results across conditions as desired.

description: Genome editing using CRISPR-Cas9 can induce specific gene correction or disruption through activation of different DNA damage repair pathways.3,4,5 The Cas9 enzyme forms a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex with a guide RNA molecule, the sequence of which can target specific genes using ∼20 nucleotides of homology to the genomic target. The RNP induces a blunt double stranded break (DSB) upon recognition and binding of the guide RNA to its target DNA sequence, and the protein-specific protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) in the target DNA to the PAM-interacting domain in the Cas9 protein.6 Staggered DNA breaks with overhangs can be generated as well by Cas12a enzymes7 and other gene editing mechanisms can be achieved by Cas9-fusion proteins such as base editing and prime editing.8,9 Cells have evolved complex mechanisms to repair DSBs, including those induced by CRISPR-Cas. DSBs are primarily resolved through the non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) pathway, which anneals the broken DNA strands with a small chance of DNA insertions and deletions at the DSB site. Perfectly repaired DNA can be targeted by CRISPR-Cas again, which leads to a cumulatively high chance of mutations at the target site.10,11,12 Alternatively, DSB can be repaired by homology-directed repair (HDR), which resects the DNA strands and uses a template DNA molecule to guide the repair. In nature, this is done by the sister chromatid during mitosis, however this process can be hijacked by delivering a synthetic DNA template to induce specific mutations. Small therapeutic mutations are often encoded on single stranded oligo deoxynucleotides (ssODN). In the context of CRISPR-Cas-mediated (therapeutic) mutations, the PAM site is often also mutated to ensure that the DNA is no longer cleavable by SpCas9.
